title: Strategies of the Warring States
subtitle: Vertical and Horizontal Alliances · The Wind and Clouds of the Strategists · The Eloquence of the Warring States
description: "Strategies of the Warring States" (Zhanguoce), compiled by Liu Xiang of the Western Han dynasty, collects the strategies and speeches of the persuaders of the Warring States period, in thirty-three chapters. It records the brilliant stories of the vertical-horizontal strategists such as Su Qin and Zhang Yi, who with their three-inch tongues swayed the great trends of the world—the strong bullying the weak, the vertical and horizontal alliances, one moment serving Qin and the next Chu. Its incisive rhetoric, superb debating skills, and vivid characters make it an encyclopedia of ancient Chinese diplomacy and strategy.

route.title: Journey Through the Strategies of the Warring States: The Stage of the Vertical-Horizontal Strategists
route.intro:
The wind whistles, the waters of the Yi River grow cold; / The brave man, once gone, will never return.
Unlike "Zuo's Commentary" with its chronological format, "Strategies of the Warring States" is organized by state, collecting the brilliant speeches of strategists who traveled to persuade the feudal lords. When Liu Xiang compiled these fragments, he remarked: "In the Warring States era, the virtue of rulers was shallow. Those who devised strategies for them had to rely on circumstances and draw plans according to the times. Their schemes were emergency measures and temporary expedients. Although they cannot be used for national governance and moral transformation, they were of urgent necessity in times of war. All of them were men of extraordinary talent who measured what their rulers could do and produced exceptional strategies, turning danger into safety, destruction into survival." Su Qin, who stabbed his thigh with an awl to stay awake studying and eventually wore the seals of six states; Zhang Yi, who deceived Chu, playing the great powers like chess pieces; Jing Ke, who tried to assassinate the King of Qin—"The wind whistles, the waters of the Yi River grow cold; the brave man, once gone, will never return"; Tang Ju, who fulfilled his mission, pitting the anger of a commoner against the anger of the Son of Heaven. Though some of these stories contain fictionalized or exaggerated elements, the wisdom and courage they embody have stirred Chinese hearts for over two thousand years. Let us enter the ruins of five Warring States capitals and experience that era of storms, when the vertical-horizontal strategists, armed only with their three-inch tongues, stirred up the realm.

stops.title: Stop One: The Lower Capital of Yan Ruins: The Starting Point of Jing Ke's Assassination Attempt
stops.content: The most famous story in the "Strategies of the Warring States—Strategies of Yan" is undoubtedly Jing Ke's assassination of the King of Qin. Crown Prince Dan of Yan had been humiliated while a hostage in the State of Qin. After returning to his own state, he was determined to take revenge. He found the swordsman Jing Ke and secured a map of the Dukang region and the head of Fan Yuqi as gifts. "The Crown Prince and all his retainers who knew of the plan, dressed in white robes and caps, saw him off. When they reached the Yi River, after the farewell ceremony, they set out. Gao Jianli played the zhu, and Jing Ke harmonized and sang, his voice in the bianzhi mode, and all the retainers wept, tears and stream mingling. Then he stepped forward and sang: 'The wind whistles, the waters of the Yi River grow cold; the brave man, once gone, will never return!' Then he sang in a stirring yu mode, and all the retainers glared with wide-open eyes, their hair standing up beneath their caps." The Lower Capital of Yan Ruins (Including Mass Burial Tombs) in Yi County, Hebei, was the Yan state's southern military stronghold during the Warring States period. The city site consists of eastern and western cities, with rammed-earth walls still standing. The Yi River once flowed nearby—standing here, you can almost imagine that autumn morning 2,300 years ago: the farewell party in white, Gao Jianli playing the zhu and singing mournfully, Jing Ke advancing fearlessly to his death. "Strategies of the Warring States" describes Jing Ke's assassination attempt with cinematic vividness: "Jing Ke took the map and presented it. When it was unrolled to the end, the dagger was revealed. He seized the King of Qin's sleeve with his left hand and stabbed at him with the dagger in his right hand. Before he could reach him, the King started back in alarm, pulling himself free, tearing his sleeve. He drew his sword, but it was long and caught in its scabbard. He was in a panic; the sword was stuck and could not be drawn immediately..." Though the assassination ultimately failed, Jing Ke's heroism has haunted the hearts of countless literati across the ages. "Strategies of the Warring States—Strategies of Yan" also records a detail that evokes profound regret—Jing Ke had been waiting for a traveling companion, but the Crown Prince's urgency forced him to depart prematurely. If he had been able to wait for that true partner, history might have been rewritten. As for Gao Jianli, who played the zhu to see off Jing Ke, he later changed his name and became a musician for the First Emperor of Qin, hiding lead in his zhu to avenge his friend, and was ultimately executed. Two assassins, with their lives, wrote the most tragic chapter of the Warring States. When the Grand Historian read this, he sighed: "From Cao Mo to Jing Ke, these five men—their righteousness may have succeeded or failed, but their purpose was clear. They did not betray their principles. Their names have been handed down to posterity—how could this be in vain!"

stops.title: Stop Two: The Ancient City of Zhao in Handan: The City of Transformation—Riding and Shooting in Barbarian Dress
stops.content: Among the Seven Powers of the Warring States, Zhao was a state founded on military might. King Wuling of Zhao implemented the policy of "riding and shooting in barbarian dress"—discarding the traditional loose robes and wide sleeves for the short jackets and trousers of the northern nomads, and learning to ride horses and shoot arrows. This was one of the most important military reforms in Chinese history, catapulting Zhao into the ranks of the only states that could contend with powerful Qin. "Strategies of the Warring States" records the activities of many Zhao strategists, the most moving being "Chu Long Persuades Queen Dowager Zhao"—the Queen Dowager was unwilling to send her beloved son, the Lord of Chang'an, as a hostage to Qi. Chu Long moved her with the words, "A parent who loves a child plans for the long term," and the old lady finally agreed to let her son serve the state. The Ancient City of Zhao in Handan is in Handan, Hebei, consisting of the Zhao King City (palace city) and the Great Northern City (outer city). Zhao made this its capital from 386 BC until its fall in 228 BC—a period of 158 years. The story of "Learning the Handan Walk" took place in this city—a young man from Yan came to Handan to learn how the Zhao people walked, but not only failed to learn, he forgot how to walk himself. Behind the humor of this idiom lies the cultural prosperity and influence of the Warring States period in Zhao. Before the Battle of Changping, Yu Qing in "Strategies of the Warring States" repeatedly urged King Xiaocheng of Zhao not to take on Qin rashly. The king refused to listen, and as a result, 400,000 Zhao troops were buried alive by Bai Qi. Standing at the ruins of the ancient city of Handan, remembering the earnest counsel of those strategists and the stubbornness of the rulers—history always repeats itself in similar errors. Among the most heart-stirring commoners of righteousness in "Strategies of the Warring States—Strategies of Zhao" is Lu Zhonglian. When Handan was besieged by Qin forces, the emissary of the King of Wei urged the King of Zhao to honor Qin as emperor and seek temporary peace. Lu Zhonglian denounced the tyranny of Qin: "As for Qin, a state that has abandoned ritual and righteousness and ranks military achievements above all else," and swore: "If Qin becomes emperor, then I, Lian, will go to the Eastern Sea and drown myself rather than become its subject." This declaration moved the Lord of Pingyuan to tears and shamed the Wei emissary into retreat. As for Lin Xiangru, his legend of "Returning the Jade Intact to Zhao" and the Mianchi Meeting—"Xiangru glared at him, and all around him cowered"—the righteous indignation of one civil official made even the tiger-like Qin yield. This is the power of the strategist: righteousness as a sword, eloquence as a blade.

stops.title: Stop Three: The Ancient City of Qi in Linzi: The Radiant Wisdom of the Jixia Academy
stops.content: The Jixia Academy of the State of Qi was the earliest government-run institution of higher learning in world history. "Strategies of the Warring States" records many strategists active in Qi—Chunyu Kun, who used a riddle to persuade King Wei of Qi: "A bird that neither flies nor calls—once it flies, it will soar to heaven; once it calls, it will astound the world"; Zou Ji, who used his own experience—"My wife favors me, my concubine fears me, my guests seek something from me"—to remonstrate with King Wei of Qi to open the channels of opinion. These stories not only show the strategists' wit but also reveal the open and inclusive political culture of Qi during the Warring States period. The Ancient City of Qi in Linzi reached its zenith in the Warring States period. When Su Qin was persuading King Xuan of Qi, he described it thus: "Linzi is extremely wealthy and substantial. Its people all play the yu and the se, beat the zhu and thrum the zither, fight quail and walk dogs, play liubo and kick football. On the streets of Linzi, cart hubs strike each other, people's shoulders rub..." This super-metropolis of 15 square kilometers was thronged with scholars, merchants, and persuaders from all states. "Strategies of the Warring States—Strategies of Qi" also contains a story with a remarkably modern feel—"Feng Xuan Serves Lord Mengchang." Feng Xuan became a retainer at Lord Mengchang's gate, but at first he only tapped his sword and sang: "My long sword, let us go home—there is no fish to eat" ... "no carriage to ride" ... "no means to support my family." Everyone looked down on him, but Lord Mengchang granted each of his requests. Later, Feng Xuan "bought righteousness" for his lord—burning the loan documents to win the people's hearts, and helping Lord Mengchang regain his position when he was dismissed as chancellor. This story teaches us that true talent often does not reveal itself from the start.

buildings.n: Qi State Ancient City in Linzi

stops.title: Stop Four: The Xianyang Qin Capital Ruins: The Rise of the Tigerish State of Qin
stops.content: In "Strategies of the Warring States," the State of Qin was the collective nightmare of the six states' strategists. Zhang Yi deceived King Huai of Chu, luring him with the promise of six hundred li of Shangyu territory to break off relations with Qi—then gave only six li. "Zhang Yi Deceives Chu" is the most famous diplomatic fraud in Warring States history. Fan Sui went to Qin and proposed the strategy of "befriending distant states while attacking those nearby," completely changing Qin's strategic direction. Li Si, with the words "Mount Tai does not reject any soil, therefore it can become great; rivers and seas do not reject any stream, therefore they can become deep," persuaded King Ying Zheng of Qin to rescind the order expelling foreign talents. The Xianyang Qin Capital Ruins are in Xianyang, Shaanxi. Duke Xiao moved the capital here, and the First Emperor of Qin expanded it on a massive scale after unifying the realm. The city stretched across both sides of the Wei River, with palaces and halls standing everywhere. Though little remains above ground today, archaeological excavations have revealed the enormous foundations of Qin Xianyang Palace No. 1—"The six kings were defeated, the four seas united; the mountains of Shu were stripped bare, and Epang Palace emerged." "Strategies of the Warring States" records of Qin are filled with fear and helplessness. Su Qin formed a vertical alliance of six states to resist Qin; Zhang Yi promoted a horizontal alliance to break the vertical league—almost all the schemes of the strategists revolved around Qin. Fan Sui's rise was itself a legend: suspected of treason by the Wei chancellor, he was beaten nearly to death, feigned death to escape, entered Qin under the pseudonym Zhang Lu, and eventually became chancellor by proposing the "befriending distant states while attacking those nearby" policy. Cai Ze later eloquently persuaded Fan Sui to yield his position, a story passed down through the ages. Shang Yang's reforms strengthened the army, Zhang Yi's deception of Chu broke the vertical alliance, Fan Sui's strategy of distant friendship and nearby attack, Li Si's advice to rescind the expulsion order—four generations of strategists working in relay, until the tigerish State of Qin finally united the realm.

buildings.n: Xianyang City Site of Qin Dynasty

stops.title: Stop Five: The Ancient City of Chu at Jinan in Jingzhou: Qu Yuan's Motherland
stops.content: During the Warring States period, Chu was the state with the most extensive territory and the one most capable of resisting Qin. "Strategies of the Warring States—Strategies of Chu" records a series of tragedies during the reign of King Huai of Chu—deceived by Zhang Yi, detained by Qin, dying in a foreign land. Qu Yuan, in his grief and indignation, wrote "Encountering Sorrow"—"Long I sigh and wipe away my tears, grieving over the hardships of the people"—and ultimately threw himself into the Miluo River when the Qin general Bai Qi captured the capital Ying. Chen Zhen came from Qin to Chu, proposing an alliance with Han and Wei against powerful Qin, but King Huai would not listen; Zhao Sui advocated resistance against Qin, clashing fiercely with the pro-Qin faction in court. The wisdom of strategists, before a benighted ruler, ultimately turned into a sigh. The Ancient City of Chu at Jinan—this southern capital, the largest metropolis of the south—was reduced to ashes after Bai Qi captured Ying. In 278 BC, the Qin general Bai Qi breached Ying, burned the Chu ancestral temples, and King Qingxiang of Chu was forced to move the capital to Chen. From then on, Chu never recovered, powerless to resist Qin any longer. The layers of ash several meters thick in the ruins are the silent testimony to that cataclysm. In the last years of the Warring States, the people of Chu issued in grief and anger the vow: "Even if Chu has only three households, it will be Qin that is destroyed"—a hundred years later, Xiang Yu, a man of Chu, indeed overthrew the tyranny of Qin. The echo of history rings with such somber power. "Strategies of the Warring States" contains a thought-provoking passage: "With the strength of Chu, none under heaven could withstand it." Yet why did such a powerful Chu ultimately fall to Qin? Because King Huai was "deluded by Zheng Xiu within and deceived by Zhang Yi without," deaf to the loyal remonstrances of Qu Yuan. The stories of the strategists teach an eternal truth: the greatest enemy is never outside, but within the court, in the heart of the sovereign. Standing on the ruins of Jinan City, watching the sun set in the west, the mists of 2,300 years still seem to linger among the broken walls. Chen Zhen in "Strategies of the Warring States" was a master persuader who moved between Qin and Chu. Using the fable of "drawing legs on a snake," he persuaded the Chu general Zhaoyang to withdraw from attacking Qi: "A man of Chu was offering a sacrifice. He gave his retainers a cup of wine... One man finished his snake first, took the wine and was about to drink, then held the cup in his left hand and drew with his right: 'I can give it legs.' Before he finished, another man finished his snake, snatched the cup and said: 'A snake has no legs. How can you add legs?' Then he drank the wine." At this, Zhaoyang understood the profound meaning that one should not add unnecessary embellishments to a completed task, and withdrew his troops. A fable of no more than a few dozen words could stop a war—such was the power of the strategist's art: four ounces shifting a thousand pounds.

stops.title: Stop Six: The Ancient City of Zhongshan: The Swan Song of a White Di Kingdom
stops.content: In the narrow space between the Seven Powers of the Warring States, there existed a mysterious kingdom known as the "Eighth Power of the Warring States"—the State of Zhongshan. "Strategies of the Warring States—Strategies of Zhongshan" records the story of this White Di state's tenacious survival amid powerful enemies. Although a Rong-Di state, Zhongshan was deeply influenced by Chinese culture, adopting the Central Plains' ritual systems and bureaucracy. Sima Guang in his "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government" commented: "Zhongshan was a separate branch of the White Di." This small state of only a few hundred li of territory survived for over a century wedged between the great powers of Zhao, Yan, and Qi—its resilience and wisdom are remarkable. The Ancient City of Zhongshan in Sanji Township, Pingshan County, Hebei, is the site of the Zhongshan capital Lingshou. The city site is an irregular rectangle, about four kilometers wide from east to west and about four and a half kilometers from north to south, with walls built of rammed earth. Archaeological excavations from 1974 to 1978 yielded world-shocking results: over ten thousand precious artifacts were unearthed from the Zhongshan king tombs, including the renowned "Three Vessels of Zhongshan"—the Zhongshan King Square Hu, the Zhongshan King Ding, and the Zhongshan King Round Hu—each bearing long inscriptions recording Zhongshan's history and achievements. Most breathtaking of all is an inlaid gold and silver bronze planchette with four dragons and four phoenixes—four divine dragons stand proudly upright, four phoenixes spread their wings as if to take flight, dragons and phoenixes intertwining in intricate patterns that take one's breath away. This is the pinnacle of Warring States bronze casting, now housed in the Hebei Provincial Museum. Also among the treasures are a fifteen-branch lotus-shaped bronze lamp, a bronze lamp with a silver-headed human figurine, and other peerless artifacts, whose craftsmanship rivals that of any Central Plains state. In 296 BC, Zhongshan was finally conquered by Zhao. But the splendid civilization of this White Di kingdom achieved immortality through those inlaid gold and silver bronzes, becoming the finest evidence of the multicultural fusion of the Warring States era.
